title: VA: More Youngkin Snitch Line Fiasco Unspools
author: Peter Greene
summary: Peter Greene follows up on Virginia Governor Glenn Youngkin's tip line for parents to report teachers over supposedly divisive instruction. He frames the line as one piece of a broader political campaign against public schools, pairing a vague anti-divisive-concepts order with a mechanism designed to intimidate teachers into silence. Greene then walks through what freedom-of-information releases actually revealed: roughly 350 emails, many frivolous, some complimentary, a few legitimate special-education complaints, and none that identified the feared indoctrination. His move is to let the underlying documents puncture the political theater, noting that the line was quietly shut down months before the governor stopped touting it. He closes by placing Virginia alongside similar failed efforts in North Carolina and hoping voters will reward fewer politicians who use teachers as props. For an archive on school culture and the teaching profession, it is a clear example of how surveillance-style policy lands on teachers.
points: Vague bans on divisive concepts predictably chill teaching because administrators avoid risk by telling teachers to steer clear of anything contentious.
The released tip-line emails showed how little real wrongdoing was reported: compliments, tutoring complaints, a complaint about Arabic numerals, and about 160 emails from one advocate.
The tip line was shut down in September when tips dried up, yet the governor kept promoting it, which Greene reads as evidence of a political stunt.
Similar teacher-reporting schemes elsewhere, such as in North Carolina, also turned up almost nothing serious.
quotes: The text is spectacularly vague, and though it contains a list of some "divisive concepts" that are specifically naughty, its reliance on that "divisive concept" language guarantees that schools across the state will have no clear idea what exactly is forbidden, and so administrations not in the mood for a fight will simply instruct teachers not to talk about race, gender, or pretty much anything that might upset anybody.

To insure that the decree carries maximum power to intimidate and silence teachers, the governor has followed the lead of states like Texas and Florida and instituted a means for parents and community members to turn in any teachers for being naughty.

By February, the tip line had been a spoof on SNL ("You know you're racist when you call the cops about a Black character in a book.") and was being flooded with fake tips. Virtually every education group in the state was calling on Youngkin to take back his executive order and shut down his snitch line. It was failing hard enough that Youngkin was using half-baked legal arguments to keep people from seeing just how bad it was, because Freedom of Information is a pain when you have information that makes your big snitch line idea look dumb.

One woman used it to send a compliment every day about individual teachers while she spent 34 days recovering from hip and back surgery. One parent complained about district-offered tutoring because it was "a potential path for unknown perverts.

The total number of emails released was 350. Virtually every email writer noted that they never got a response from the Governor's office. And it appears that many not-very-serious submissions were not released.

Youngkin was still touting the tip line last week, despite the fact that it was actually shut down back in September as tips just kind of "dried up." It's almost as if this attempt to root out Critical Race Theory throughout Virginia turned up nothing. Kind of like the whole thing was just a political stunt.
